analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to reveal their donors and closes loopholes for foreign money in elections.
analysis.headline: Every Senate Democrat and independent backed the bill, but a 49-49 test vote on September 22, 2022 fell far short of the 60 votes needed to bring it to the floor, and it never got an up-or-down vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would require corporations, labor unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt 'social welfare' groups to report political spending of more than $10,000 within 24 hours and to name the people who paid for it. Political ads would have to identify their top funders on screen, and CEOs would have to personally 'approve this message.' It would also tighten the ban on foreign money in elections, extend it to digital ads and judicial-nomination campaigns, and make it a five-year felony to set up a shell company to hide foreign election money.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters watching campaign ads, who would learn who actually paid for them, and enforcement of the existing ban on foreign money in elections, which currently relies on disclosure that dark-money channels can evade.

how_it_helps.text: Groups spending more than $10,000 on elections would have to file a report with the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, naming anyone who gave them $10,000 or more, under penalty of perjury.

Political ads would have to display their top five funders on screen (top two for radio), and the CEO or top official of the sponsoring organization would have to say 'I approve this message' by name and title.

The bill extends the existing ban on foreign money to paid digital ads, to spending on ballot initiatives, to paid internet activity supporting or attacking candidates, and to campaigns for or against federal judicial nominations, where no disclosure rules exist today.

It would be a federal crime punishable by up to five years in prison to create or use a corporation with the intent to conceal foreign money in an election, closing the kind of scheme the FEC found in a 2021 case where a consultant arranged a $2 million foreign contribution routed through shell nonprofits to a super PAC.
The Government Accountability Office would have to study and report on the incidence of illicit foreign money in each presidential election cycle, including whether it targeted specific communities.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt groups that spend on elections would bear compliance costs and would lose the ability to influence elections without their funders being named. Large digital platforms would face new political-ad obligations.

drawbacks.text: The disclosure rules reach tax-exempt civic groups of all kinds, not just business PACs, so issue advocacy groups on the left and right would have to hand the FEC the names of their largest donors, which critics argue chills participation and exposes supporters to harassment. The bill contains an exception only where disclosure would subject a person to serious threats, harassment, or reprisals.

The ad-disclaimer rules would put a CEO's face and name on videos a company funded, and require top-funder lists inside short digital ads, raising free-speech and practical objections from groups across the political spectrum.

The disclosure provisions were set to take effect January 1, 2023 even if the FEC had not yet written the required regulations, which compliance experts could reasonably call an unworkable timeline for regulated groups.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and narrow: voters would know who pays for election ads, which the Supreme Court itself has called a less restrictive alternative to limiting political speech. The main cost falls on organizations that spend on politics, including charities' advocacy arms and unions, whose donors and dues-payers would become publicly identified; the bill's threat and reprisal exception softens but does not eliminate that privacy concern. On balance the bill trades anonymity for information about who is trying to influence elections and judges.

outcome.mechanism: A test vote to start debate fell short at 49-49, far below the 60 votes needed to cut off a filibuster, so the bill never got to the Senate floor for real debate or an up-or-down vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 12, 2022 with 49 cosponsors — 47 of 48 Senate Democrats and both independents — and was placed directly on the Senate calendar, skipping committee.

On September 22, 2022, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 49-49, with 47 Democrats and both independents voting yes and 49 of 50 Republicans voting no; because moving forward required 60 senators, the bill never reached the floor for debate or a vote.
Congress ended January 3, 2023, and the bill died without ever getting an up-or-down vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The organizations and donors who spend on elections without disclosure kept the status quo: an estimated $1.05 billion in dark money flowed in the 2020 cycle, and none of it became traceable. Senators also avoided an on-the-record vote on disclosure itself, since the roll call was only on whether to begin debate.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill straight to the Senate calendar, made the motion to proceed, and forced the September 22, 2022 vote on starting debate.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 47 of them voted to start debate.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and both voted to start debate.

against.what_they_did: Voted no on the September 22, 2022 cloture vote on the motion to proceed, denying the 60 votes needed to begin debate and keeping the bill off the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Every Democrat and independent who voted (49 senators) voted yes and every Republican who voted (49 senators) voted no; the tally was 49-49, with the missing 60th vote never in reach in a chamber split 50-50.

industries.note: These groups spent an estimated $1.05 billion in the 2020 cycle without naming donors; the bill would force them to report any payment of $10,000 or more used for politics within 24 hours and to put their top funders on their ads. Their core interest in anonymity runs directly against the voter's interest in knowing who is paying.

industries.industry: Corporations and super PACs that spend on elections
industries.note: Covered organizations would have to file FEC reports within 24 hours of crossing $10,000 in political spending, list beneficial owners, and have their CEOs personally approve ads on camera. The bill does not limit their spending, only its secrecy, but secrecy is what donors paid for.

Creating or using a company to conceal foreign election money would become a federal crime carrying up to five years in prison, a direct legal threat to a service that foreign-money schemes have relied on.

Unions are 'covered organizations' under the bill and would face the same 24-hour disclosure and top-funder ad rules as corporations, though transfers funded by members' dues are attributed to the members. Unions have publicly favored disclosure in general but would bear real compliance costs here.

industries.industry: Large digital advertising platforms (50 million or more U.S. users)
industries.note: Platforms above a 50-million-user threshold would face extended foreign-money prohibitions and ad-disclaimer rules, including hyperlink requirements in short ads. They would keep selling political ads but under new compliance burdens.
